==Problem==
In the figure below, each circle will be filled with a digit from 1 to 6. Each digit must appear exactly once. The sum of the digits in neighboring circles is shown in the box between them. What digit must be placed in the top circle?

[[File:2026 amc 8 q12.png | 650px]]

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 2\qquad\textbf{(B) } 3\qquad\textbf{(C) } 4\qquad\textbf{(D) } 5\qquad\textbf{(E) } \text{it is impossible to fill the circles}</imath>

==Solution==

Let <imath>O</imath> denote an odd number and <imath>E</imath> denote an even. Then, we know that <imath>O+E = O</imath>, and thus the two neighboring circles that form sums 9 and 5 must be one of each odd and even. To obtain 5, we have <imath>1+4</imath> or <imath>2+3</imath>. To obtain 9, we have <imath>3+6</imath>, <imath>4+5</imath>. Consider each case separately.

Case 1: If <imath>1+4</imath> makes the sum of 5, then the two numbers that make 9 must be <imath>3+6</imath>. Then, 3 is forced on top, and we require another 3. However, the problem doesn't allow this, so this is impossible.

Case 2: <imath>2+3</imath> is on 5, meaning that <imath>4+5</imath> is on 9. Then, we have two subcases.

Case A: 4 is on top. Then, we require 2 to complete the sum of 6, which is not possible as <imath>2+3</imath> is on 5.

Case B: 5 is on top, meaning that we require 1 right below, 3 on the bottom right, 2 to complete the sum of 5, and the rest are uniquely determined.

The number is <imath>\boxed{5}</imath>.

~Pinotation

==Solution 2==
In the bottom-left corner, we have 2 numbers that add up to 10 filled in from the digits from <imath>1</imath> to <imath>6</imath>. There are two ways you can do this, <imath>5</imath> and <imath>5</imath> or <imath>6</imath> and <imath>4</imath>. Since we can only use each integer once, the first case doesn't work, so we must have the second case. Now we need to figure out the ordering. If we have <imath>4</imath> by the <imath>8</imath>, the other circle must be <imath>4</imath>, but again, we can only use each positive integer once, so the <imath>6</imath> must be by the <imath>8</imath>, and the <imath>4</imath> must be by the <imath>10</imath> and the <imath>9</imath>. Notice that we can already find the number that needs to go into the circle we want, which is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }5}</imath> since <imath>9-4=5</imath>. ~Baihly2024

==Solution 3==
We do trial and error, and because it is a shorter problem it doesn’t take long. we can find that the only possibility is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }5}</imath>。

~pereena

==Solution 4 (Prob the fastest) ==

Let's set space 1 to the top, space 2 to the middle left, space 3 to the middle right, space 4 to the bottom left, space 5  to the bottom middle, and space 6 to the bottom right. Note that I am only doing this to better explain this to you, the numbering of spaces is just a waste of time on the AMC 8.

Look at space 3 and space 6. The numbers must sum to 4. The two numbers cannot be 2 and 2, as each digit must repeat only once, therefore the only number pair that satisfies this is 1 and 3. Now we must figure out where to place these numbers. We can now look at space 1 and space 3. If we say that space 3 is equal to 1, then space 1 must be equal to 5. That is one possible solution. Now, if we made space 3 equal to 3 instead, space 1 must be equal to 3 as well, which contradicts the problem. Therefore, the only possible solution is 5. Now, we must check and solve the rest of the triangle to make sure that there is a solution, and the answer is not E. We can now find that the final answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }5}</imath>.

~apmathematician
